content: 1. Guidelines for the use of antiretroviral drugs in treating and preventing HIV infection emphasize the importance of addressing co-infections, comorbidities, and other health conditions that are common among people living with HIV. These factors influence the timing and choice of antiretroviral therapy (ART). 2. The document provides an overview of the most common and significant conditions affecting people with HIV, summarizing key recommendations from existing WHO guidelines. It focuses on screening, prophylaxis, and the timing of ART initiation for these conditions, without delving into broader management strategies. 3. Recommendations are supported by evidence and rationale, with their strength and quality rated using the GRADE system (strong or conditional recommendations, and high, moderate, low, or very low-quality evidence) or an earlier grading system (A to C for strength and I to IV for evidence level). 4. Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) is an integral part of HIV-related care, aimed at preventing opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis, and bacterial infections, as well as providing benefits for malaria prophylaxis. Recommendations for initiating and discontinuing CPT are outlined for various populations, including adults, adolescents, pregnant women, and children. 5. CPT should be initiated in HIV-exposed infants starting at 4–6 weeks of age and continued until the risk of HIV transmission ends or HIV infection is excluded. Monitoring should occur at three-month intervals. 6. Contraindications to CPT include severe allergy to sulfa drugs, severe liver or renal disease, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. CPT should also be discontinued in cases of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, severe liver disease, severe anemia, pancytopenia, or confirmed negative HIV status. 7. Tuberculosis (TB) is the most frequent life-threatening opportunistic infection among people living with HIV and a leading cause of death. ART should be provided to all individuals with HIV and active TB disease, regardless of CD4 count. 8. The WHO Three I’s strategy for TB management in HIV care settings includes intensified TB case-finding, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), and infection control measures at all clinical encounters. 9. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those reporting symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. 10. Children living with HIV who exhibit symptoms such as poor weight gain, fever, or cough, or have a history of contact with a TB case, should be evaluated for TB. If TB is excluded, they should receive IPT regardless of age. 11. TB patients with known HIV-positive status or those living in high HIV-prevalence settings should receive at least six months of rifampicin-based treatment. Daily dosing is recommended during both the intensive and continuation phases. 12. The Xpert MTB/RIF diagnostic test should be used as the initial diagnostic tool for individuals suspected of having HIV-associated TB or multidrug-resistant TB. 13. IPT should be offered to adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB, regardless of their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, or history of TB treatment. A minimum of six months of IPT is recommended, with 36 months suggested for those with positive tuberculin skin test (TST) status. 14. TST is not required for initiating IPT, but it can be used where feasible to identify individuals who may benefit more from IPT. Concerns about isoniazid resistance should not prevent the provision of IPT. 15. Children living with HIV who are older than 12 months and unlikely to have active TB based on symptom screening should receive six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. Infants under 12 months should only receive IPT if they have a history of household contact with a TB case and active TB has been excluded. 16. All children living with HIV should receive an additional six months of isoniazid after completing TB treatment. 17. Infection control measures are critical in healthcare and congregate settings to reduce the risk of Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission. National TB and HIV programs should provide managerial direction for implementing TB infection control programs. 18. Healthcare workers living with HIV should receive ART and IPT if eligible. Protective measures, such as particulate respirator masks (e.g., N95), and relocation to lower-risk areas should be considered. 19. ART should be initiated in all TB patients, including those with drug-resistant TB, regardless of CD4 count. Antituberculosis treatment should begin first, followed by ART within the first eight weeks of TB treatment. For patients with profound immunosuppression (CD4 < 50 cells/mm³), ART should start within the first two weeks. 20. Efavirenz is the preferred NNRTI for patients starting ART while on antituberculosis treatment.
